sentences.text: Commentary § 10.4:1 Rule 10.4 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Test Under Old Rule 625 Applies to R.
10.4 with an exception In Toliver v.
Koepke, 2017 ABQB 686, 2017 CarswellAlta 2343, Justice Macklin said: 39 Rule 10.4 is the new version of r 625 of the old Rules of Court.
No case appears to have yet considered r 10.4.
However, r 10.4's requirements reflect the test Alberta courts developed for granting charging orders under r 625 (see Royal Bank of Canada v Laughlin, 2001 ABCA 78 at para 34, 277 AR 201).
Please note under the heading 4. — “action conducted by the lawyer” that Madam Justice Price has set out a material change in the new Rule.
When must the prerequisite of “will not be or are unlikely to be paid” be established?
In Paragon Capital Corporation Ltd v.
Starke Dominion Ltd, 2020 ABCA 216, 2020 CarswellAlta 979, 6 Alta.
L.R.

224 a trial judge granted a law firm a conditional charging order before the law firm could satisfactorily demonstrate “that its fees would not be or were unlikely to be paid unless the charging order was granted.” The conditional charging order was subsequently made final.
One of the issues before the Court of Appeal was whether an order under R.
10.4 can only be made if the prerequisite set out in R.
10.4(2)(a) is established at the time the application is made.
The majority of the Court held that a court may allow the requirement set out in R.
10.4(2)(a) to be satisfied “within a reasonable time subsequently.” The majority of the Court said: [32] A conflict therefore arises between r 10.4(2), and rr 1.4(1) and 9.18(1).
There is nothing explicit in the rule requiring evidence of meeting its requirements in advance of making the application for or as a condition of the granting of a charging order.

There is an ambiguity in r 10.4(2) as to whether the mandatory requirements it contains are a prerequisite to the granting of a charging order or may be met through conditions to be satisfied subsequently.
The use of the word “only” does not convey any inference as to timing.

This conflict cannot therefore be resolved simply by interpreting the phrase “may only be made if” in r 10.4(2) to mean that the requirements it imposes must be satisfied in advance. … [51] We therefore conclude that the purpose of r 10.4(2) would be best met by permitting the 10.4(2)(a) requirement to be established at the time of bringing the application for a charging order, or within a reasonable time subsequently … 3.

Application of Rule Rule 625(1) states that the solicitor is “entitled to charge upon the property recovered or preserved through his instrumentality …” The charge is only upon that property which is salvaged by the solicitor's actions … The thrust of the rule is that only the specific property which is salvaged is subject to the solicitor's charge.
It is for this reason that it must be specific and identifiable.
Furthermore, in order to be properly recovered or preserved, there must be some dispute as to its ownership.
The following statement of the rule by Sir George Jessel M.R. in Foxon v.
Gascoigne (1874), 9 Ch.
App.
654, was affirmed as providing the best guide to the meaning of the statute by the English Court of Appeal in Till v.

558 at 567 …: it means that where the plaintiff claims property, and establishes a right to the ownership of the property in some shape or other, there the property has been recovered; that where a defendant's right to the ownership of property is disputed, and that right has been vindicated by the proceedings, there the property has been preserved … recovery and preservation are correlative terms, … they both relate to the ownership of the property.
Jackson, Arlette, MacIver & Skitsko v.
Western Crane Service Ltd.
L.R.
Solicitors cannot use the rule to place a charge upon funds advanced to the solicitors by a non-client party interested in the litigation.

The portion of that judgment under appeal is his order granting the respondent Field & Field a charging order with respect to moneys advanced to it by a party interested in the prosecution and outcome of litigation being carried on by the respondent Field & Field on behalf of McCready Products Ltd.
It must be emphasized that the party advancing the money was not a party to that litigation.
It is conceded that the funds in issue were wholly used in the prosecution of the litigation.

In our respectful view the facts and supporting documents clearly show that the respondents bear no legal or ethical obligation to the party advancing the money for the use of that money other than to prosecute the claim presently before us.
They have done this with competence, enthusiasm and vigour.
The purpose of R.
625 is to protect solicitors in situations where they cannot recover their proper fees and disbursements from their client.
In our view the rule should not be extended to protect persons in the position of Hunter Douglas, the party advancing the money herein.
McCready Products Ltd. v.
Sherwin-Williams Co. of Canada (1986), 45 Alta.
L.R.
Specific, Not General, Assets The problem with charging the general assets of the company is that R.
625 only allows the specific property recovered or preserved to be charged.
As it is not possible to follow the specific assets which may have been preserved as against each of the creditors, R.
625 does not allow for a general charge against all of the assets of the company in this situation.
Jackson, Arlette, MacIver & Skitsko v.
Western Crane Service Ltd., supra, at 160.
5. “action conducted by the lawyer” In Robertson LLP v.
Pasco (Edmonton, QB Action 1901-14596
October 21, 2019

E-File No.: CVQ19ROBERTSON), both an attachment order application under section 17(2) of the Civil Enforcement Act, and a charging order application under Rule 10.4, were made on behalf of a law firm (Robertson LLP).
In those applications a number of facts were alleged which can be summarized as follows.
It was alleged that Mr.
Pasco retained a lawyer (Robertson) to act for him in the purchase of a home which was in foreclosure.
On September 13, 2019, Mr.
Pasco provided to Mr.
Robertson what purported to be a certified cheque which was deposited into Mr.
Robertson's trust account.
However, the cheque was dated October 13, 2019.
No one noticed that.
On September 16, 2019, funds to complete the purchase were transferred from Mr.
Robertson's trust account.
The purchase deal “closed”.
On September 30, 2019, Mr.
Robertson was notified that the “certified cheque”“was no good”.
On October 7, 2019, a new “certified cheque” (also bearing the date September 19, 2019) was supplied by Mr.
Pasco.
On October 15, Mr.
Robertson was advised by the bank that the second cheque was also “NSF”.
The allegation was that the “certification” of the cheques was the result of fraud.
Both applications were granted with oral reasons.

With respect to the charging order application under Rule 10.4, and in particular the phrase “the action conducted by the lawyer on the client's behalf” as set out in Rule 10.4(2)(b)(i), counsel submitted that: “And if your familiarity is only with the old rule 625, you're thinking, well, that needs to be a court action, but it's not defined, that not made clear in the rule, and—and by ‘action’ I think you can consider that as something that the lawyer has done on the client's behalf. …” Madam Justice Price said: “I agree with your interpretation, Mr.
Alcock, that an ‘action’ can be whatever conduct by the lawyer.

It doesn't have to be the litigation itself with an action number, and it's small ‘A’ action. …” Her Ladyship later said: … In addition, with respect to the charge—charging order pursuant to 10.4, I find that in this case 10.4 does apply notwithstanding the old rule.

I find that the new rule is much more expansive and was intended to be so, permitting not just barristers but solicitors in—in pursuit of what they were intending to secure, and specifically looking at the test, I find that rule 10.4 permits a lawyer to apply to the Court and secure a charging order over assets of a client, provided the lawyer can satisfy the following requirements:
(a) the lawyer must have acted on behalf of the client
(b) the lawyer's efforts must have resulted or preserved for the client the net property sought to be charged
(c) the charge is limited to fees and disbursements incurred in the act or by the work which recovered or preserved—by the work of the lawyer which recovered or preserved the property
(d) even if the foregoing conditions are met, the Court may not grant the charge if to do so would be unfair.
In this case, I find it fair to grant it.
This is a material departure from the old Rule 625.

Rule Is Based on Principle of Salvage Although referred to as a “solicitor's lien”, the charge provided for is really a right to protection by interference by the court against a solicitor being left unpaid (Feehan v.
Pocock Floors Ltd., [1971] 4 W.W.R.
572 at 573 (Alta.
Dist.
Ct.); Jackson v.
Western Crane Service Ltd., [1984] 33 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 157 (Q.B.)), and is based on the principle of salvage whereby salvor is rewarded for having preserved something in a time of danger.
The court has a discretion whether to enforce the lien.

Because the protection granted is protection for the solicitor and not for the client, the court may refuse to enforce it unless the solicitor establishes at least to a prima facie extent, that he or she will be unable to collect his or her costs from the client (Phillipps & Scarth v.
London Guar. & Accident Co., 36 Man.
R.
McCready Products Ltd. v.
Sherwin-Williams Co. of Canada (1986), 43 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 269 (Q.B.), at 273, per Wachowich J.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal from Wachowich J.'s decision [see (1986), 45 Alta.
L.R.
However, the Court of Appeal did not criticize the above statement.
Indeed, at p.
229, the court said: The purpose of R.
625 is to protect solicitors in situations where they cannot recover their proper fees and disbursements from their client.
Trust Agreement to Return Funds Will Negative a Lien Mr.
Jamison, a barrister and solicitor, was placed in funds by Alberta Transportation (a Ministry of the Government of Alberta) on certain trust conditions.

The final condition was, and I quote: That you will return any funds not advanced or disbursed to Alberta Transportation upon ten days' notice being given. … Assuming that one could classify the moneys to be returned as a “fund” for the purposes of R.
625, the indisputable fact here is that, in the trust conditions agreed to by him, the lawyer agreed that he would return all of it.
There is an express agreement by him which negatives any solicitor's lien claim and also any claim (as a trustee of the fund) for services in connection with the administration of it.
We reject the argument so eloquently put by Mr.
Major that we ought to infer that the express trust condition in the letter was subject to an implied term that he may deduct his fees.
We are loath to impart such terms into express trust conditions respecting moneys sent to a lawyer.
Jamison v.
Alberta Transportation (1987), 53 Alta.
L.R.
Two Types of Liens In this jurisdiction there are two types of solicitor's liens: those arising from a charging order on property recovered or preserved by the solicitor under R.
625 and those arising from the solicitor's possession of the client's documents or property.
The latter, known as a retaining lien, is the type of lien in issue in this appeal.
A retaining lien is defined by Evershed M.R. in Barratt v.
Gough-Thomas, [1951] Ch.
242 (C.A.): The nature of a solicitor's general retaining lien has more than once been authoritatively stated.
It is a right at common law depending, it has been said, on implied agreement.
It has not the character of an encumbrance or equitable charge.
It is merely passive and possessory, that is to say, the solicitor has no right of actively enforcing his demand.
It confers on him merely the right to withhold possession of the documents or other personal property of his client or former client—in the words of Sir E.
Sugden in Blunden v.
Desart (2) (2 Dr. & War.

418): … to lock them up in his box, and to put the key into his pocket, until his client satisfies the amount of the demand It is wholly derived from, and, therefore, co-extensive with, the right of the client to the documents or other property: see the statement of Lord Cranworth, L.J., in Pelly v.
Wathen… cited by Chitty, J., in Re Llewellin, [1891] 3 Ch.
Imperial Developments (Canada) Ltd.
(Receiver of) v.
Field & Field (1988), 59 Alta.
L.R.

And Mason J. said: The Rule 625 type of lien gives the court the power to declare counsel entitled to a charge “on anything recovered by judgment resulting from his or her labour and professional services”.
[The Canadian Law Dictionary, (Law and Business Publications: Don Mills, 1980) at 355].
Counsel must specifically apply for a solicitor's lien under Rule 625.
The court may grant a charge against property which has been salvaged because of counsel's efforts.
The retaining lien allows counsel to withhold documents in his or her possession from his or her client, or anyone else claiming under that client, until counsel has been paid.
This passive retaining lien arises out of equity and exists as long as counsel withholds his or her client's documents.
White Resource Management Ltd. v.
Durish (1997), 54 Alta.
L.R.
In Merchant Law Group v.
McLeod & Co., 2005 ABQB 875, 2005 CarswellAlta 2014, 55 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 301, Rawlins J., at pp.

306–322, provided the following exhaustive and very helpful overview (and suggests there are really three types of lien): Though it is perhaps not commonly recognized by the legal community, there are three types of liens or charges upon which a solicitor may rely to obtain payment of his fees.
Retaining Lien Of these three, the most widely understood is what is sometimes referred to as the “retaining lien”.
In the recent case of Cochard, Re, 2005 ABQB 679 (Alta.
Q.B.), Veit J. described this lien at para.
60 as “a common law lien allowing [a] lawyer to hold client documents, in much the same way as a mechanic can hold a car until the repair bill is paid”.
In an older but still instructive and often referenced work, The Law and Practice Relating to Solicitor's Liens and Charging Orders (London: Sweet and Maxwell, 1905), F.W.
Atkinson described this lien (which he referred to as a “lien on documents”) at p.

2 as a “passive lien”, meaning that “the solicitor has no right of selling or otherwise realising the property subject to the lien or charge, but has the bare right of detaining or remaining in possession of the property until his claim is satisfied”.

This type of lien is commonly asserted by practitioners who retain a client's file and refuse to transfer it to a subsequent solicitor until satisfactory arrangements have been made for payment of the prior solicitor's account.
Such arrangements are often made through trust conditions agreed to between the solicitors. . . . . .

Charges on Property in Possession of Another Party It is less commonly understood that there are two other methods by which a solicitor may impose a charge for his fees on property in the possession of another party.
One arises at common law, the other by statute.
There is little consistency in the case law in the terminology used to describe these charges, in large part because many of the cases fail to draw a distinction between the two.
For purposes of this analysis, I shall refer to the common law charge as a “charging lien”, to the statutory charge as a “charging order” and to the two of them collectively as “charges”.

Many solicitors are familiar with the charging order that may be obtained from this Court pursuant to Rule 625, … As Veit J. pointed out in Cochard, Re, this Rule provides a mechanism for a solicitor to obtain the kind of charge contemplated by s.
28 of the English Solicitors Act, 1860, which statute continues to be law in Alberta.15 Prior to the creation of this statutory charging order, solicitors could rely upon a common law charging lien.
That lien has been described as “a claim to the equitable interference of the Court to have [a] judgment held as a security for [the solicitor's] debt” (per Parke, B., in Barker v.
St.
Quintin (1844), 152 E.R.
Exch.), at 1274 as quoted by Henry J. in Tots & Teens Sault Ste.
Marie Ltd., Re (1975), 11 O.R.
Bktcy.), at 107).
At p.

3, Atkinson describes the origin of this lien (which he refers to as a “lien on funds”) as follows: The law of solicitors' lien is derived from the common law and the practice of the Courts of equity, and not from any statutes.
It is not very ancient; indeed, according to Lord St.
Leonards [citation omitted], it is comparatively modern, and Mr.

Whitley Stokes in his admirable work says that the earliest reported case in favour of the lien on documents is in the reign of James II., and the first case relating to the lien on funds much later; but before the end of the eighteenth century, the lien of solicitors, both on documents and funds, was well established both at law and in equity.
The charging order and the charging lien have a number of features in common.
First, neither is, properly speaking, a “lien” at all as neither involves the retention of property by the person asserting the claim.
Henry J. in Tots & Teens referred with approval to the following quote from Lord Goddard, C.J. of the English Court of Appeal, in James Bibby Ltd. v.
Woods, [1949] 2 K.B.
K.B.), at 453: A solicitor has a lien on papers of his clients which are in his possession; he can refuse to give up those papers so long as his costs are not paid.
He is also commonly said to have a lien on a sum of money which comes into existence owing to his exertions, but in that case the term “lien” is really a misnomer.
The solicitor's right in that case is not strictly and accurately a lien because it has not the characteristics of a lien.
That was made clear by Cockburn C.J. in Mercer v.
Graves, L.R.
7 Q.B.

499, 503, in which he said: “There is no such thing as a lien except upon something of which you have possession … although we talk of an attorney having a lien upon a judgment, it is in fact only a claim or right to ask for the intervention of the court for his protection, when, having obtained judgment for his client, he finds there is a probability of the client depriving him of his costs.” Second, both the charging order and the charging lien, in contrast to the passive retaining lien, are “active” in nature.

While the retaining lien entitles a solicitor only to refuse to release his file until his fees are paid, both the charging order and the charging lien entitle him to take action to obtain payment of those fees.
In light of the similarities between them, it is tempting to think that the charging order and the charging lien are one and the same.
It is clear, however, that they are conceptually distinct.
Veit J. in Cochard, Re, ¶ 67 quoted parts of Atkinson's summary at pp.

9–11 of the distinctions between the two: In the first place it will be observed that the operation of a charging order under the Act very closely resembles the lien on funds which we have seen was established by the Courts of law and equity quite a hundred years before the Act was passed, but we must not allow ourselves to be led astray by this resemblance.

The two things are perfectly distinct in their origin, their subject-matter, as to the persons who can obtain them, the persons against whom they can be obtained or asserted, and the grounds of resistance.

The following noteworthy differences will be found in the succeeding chapters:—until the charging order is actually pronounced there is no charge in existence; in the words of Lord Selborne in Pinkerton v.

Easton[citation omitted], “The Legislature has not given a charge, but a power to the Court to create a charge, for a solicitor's costs, upon property recovered or preserved, when meritorious services of the solicitor have resulted in such recovery or preservation.” A lien on funds, on the contrary, is acquired by the solicitor ipso facto the moment property has been recovered or preserved by his proceedings [citation omitted].
Again, a charging order can be made on real estate, whereas a lien cannot be claimed against it [citation omitted].
A town agent cannot get the charging order; he can assert a lien: The granting or refusing a charging order is in the discretion of the Court, whereas a lien is ex debito justitiae.
It is true that a lien is “an application to the equitable interference of the Court,” but still that interference is always exercised in a proper case as a matter of right.

A charging order will be made only on the net balance coming to the client or party benefited: whereas there are cases in which the Court has refused to allow a set-off to be opposed to the solicitor's lien even since the coming into operation of Order LXV. r.14, of the Rules of 1883.

When making a charging order or afterwards the Court has power to provide for the raising and payment of what is due to the solicitor by sale of the property or otherwise, whereas there is no decision to the effect that it can do this in aid of a solicitor's lien, though it can in such a case direct money owing to the client to be paid to the solicitor either by the opposite party or out of a fund in Court.

A charging order will be made only to secure costs incurred in any Court of justice, whereas a solicitor has the lien on moneys recovered by proceedings before arbitrators, even where the submission has not been made a rule of Court.

On applying for a charging order it is not necessary to prove either express notice of the solicitor's lien or collusion, but to successfully assert a lien either notice of the lien or collusion must be proved.

The charge created by an order is always special—that is, it can only be given to secure the costs in that particular proceeding in which the property was recovered or preserved, and cannot be extended to the general balance of account, or even to costs in other matters.
A lien, on the other hand, may sometimes be general, for instance as between town agent and country solicitor [citation omitted].
Last, but not least, the Statute of Limitations is a fatal answer to an application for a charging order, whereas it does not prejudice the lien on funds in any shape or form.

It will be seen from these differences that in some cases the charging order is more favourable to the solicitor than the lien, whereas in other instances the lien is more beneficial than the charging order.

Criteria for Granting a Charge … It appears that one of the prerequisites for a charge is that the solicitor must show a prima facie case that he will be unable to obtain payment of fees unless the charge is granted.
Wachowich J., as he then was, in considering a Rule 625 charging order in McCready Products Ltd. v.
Sherwin-Williams Co. of Canada (1986), 68 A.R.
342 (Alta.
Q.B.); reversed on other grounds (1986), 45 Alta.
L.R.
C.A.), held at para.

10 that “[b]ecause the protection granted is protection for the solicitor and not for the client, the court may refuse to enforce it unless the solicitor establishes at least to a prima facie extent, that he or she will be unable to collect his or her costs from the client.” A similar requirement appears to apply in the case of a charging lien, as demonstrated by comment from Cockburn C.J. in Mercer v.
Graves (1872), L.R.
7 Q.B.

Q.B.) (quoted in Tots & Teens at 107) that this lien allows a solicitor to ask for the assistance of the court “when, having obtained judgment for his client, he finds there is a probability of the client depriving him of his costs.” … Property Subject to Charge In addition to their other similarities, the charging order and the charging lien share a common “specific” nature.
In this regard, Atkinson makes the following comments at p.
2: A lien may be either special or general.

A general lien is a lien to secure, not only the debt incurred in the particular matter in which the property subject to the lien was obtained, or recovered, but also to secure all other debts and the general balance of account. …[A] solicitor has, as a general rule, subject to but a few exceptions, a general lien on documents, but only a special lien on funds [citation omitted], and in the case of the statutory charging order only a special charge on the specific property recovered or preserved.
As special liens, the charging order and the charging lien are limited in two respects.
First, only certain property may be impressed with the charge.
Second, the charge extends only to certain debts.
However, though both are special liens, there are differences between the charging order and the charging lien in terms of their attachments to property.

By its terms, Rule 625 limits the property that may be subject to a charging order to “the property recovered or preserved through [the solicitor's] instrumentality in any proceeding prosecuted or defended by him.” This wording has been held to give rise to a number of limitations which were enumerated by the Alberta Court of Appeal as follows in Royal Bank v.
Laughlin 277 A.R.
(a) the lawyer must have conducted litigation on behalf of the client
(b) the lawyer's efforts in the litigation must have recovered or preserved for the client the net property sought to be charged
(c) the charge is limited to fees and disbursements incurred in the same litigation which recovered or preserved the property
(d) even if the foregoing conditions are met, the court may not grant the charge if to do so would be unfair.
By contrast, Atkinson states at p.

44 that “[t]he [charging] lien attaches on whatever is coming to a client at the close of the proceedings in which he has employed the solicitor professionally.” This is somewhat broader in scope, though it is clear from the commentary that certain property, such as land, cannot be attached in this manner.
Returning to charging orders, the first limitation set out in Laughlin requires that the solicitor have conducted litigation on behalf of the client.

There is case law to the effect that this requires a court action to have been initiated and that negotiations in the absence of such an action are insufficient to ground a claim for a charging order.
See, for example, Home Assurance Co. of Canada, Re (1949), [1950] 1 D.L.R.
611, (Alta.
T.D.); aff'd.
511 (Alta.
C.A.). … By contrast, a solicitor's entitlement to a charging lien is not restricted to matters in which the solicitor has conducted litigation.
Atkinson states at p.

44 that “This lien applies, not only to hostile actions, but to friendly proceedings as well, e.g. administration, partition, partnership, and other actions”. … The second Laughlin criterion for a charging order requires that property have been recovered or preserved through the solicitor's instrumentality.

The charging lien does not appear at first glance to be subject to this requirement, but, as Atkinson notes, it is particular to the “fruits” of the action or other proceeding in which the solicitor is professionally engaged, those fruits being the debt, damages, fund in Court or other monies recovered in that action or other proceeding.
Thus, the two charges appear to be quite similar in this regard.

Both Respondents directed some of their argument toward the question of what efforts had been expended by the Applicant in furtherance of the clients' cases and took the position that those efforts were not sufficient to ground a claim for any kind of charge on the proceeds of the lawsuits.
I am not prepared to accede to that argument.

There is nothing in the wording of Rule 625 or in the cases and commentaries with respect to charging liens that requires a prior solicitor to have done a specified amount of work before becoming entitled to a charging order or charging lien.
If a solicitor can demonstrate that he has done some work on the matter in question, the charge may be granted, subject of course to the other restrictions.
The amount of fees and disbursements to which he is entitled is then a matter for taxation.
It is not the job of this Court on this application to determine the worth of Merchant Law Group's efforts once they have crossed the minimum threshold.
Further argument in respect of the property to which a charge can attach was directed to whether a charging order or charging lien can be maintained in the context of a contingency fee arrangement.
In this Province, there are two competing judgments on this point: Law Firm v.
Solicitor, [1992] A.J.
No.
1242 (Alta.
Q.B.), a decision of O'Leary J.
(as he then was) and Client v.
Law Firm, 254 A.R.
Q.B.), a decision of Marceau J.

It is important to note that in both of these cases, release of the prior solicitor's file was sought; therefore, the type of lien at issue was the retaining lien and the Court in both cases appeared to pay little heed to the distinction between a charging order and a charging lien.
Nevertheless, because all of the matters at issue here were subject to contingency fee arrangements, the cases are relevant.
In the older case, O'Leary J. referred to the case of Baergen v.
Peterson Ross (1986), 74 A.R.
230 (Alta.
Q.B.) in which Berger J.
(as he then was) held that it was not possible to tax a contingency fee account prior to the conclusion of the file.
O'Leary J. went on to find that a solicitor could not assert a lien for fees prior to the conclusion of a contingency file and made the following comments at paras.

11, 13 and 16: In my view, where the client has agreed as part of the contingency arrangement to pay the disbursements involved in prosecuting the litigation in any event, there is no reason why the common law solicitor's lien need be displaced in respect of those disbursements.
With respect to the fee portion of the solicitor's account, it is apparent that a solicitor's lien is inconsistent with that arrangement.
It cannot be asserted where the solicitor is discharged or withdraws before the conclusion of the matter, that is before his entitlement to a contingent fee has been determined. . . . . .
The lien in respect of fees in a contingency arrangement is inappropriate and does not exist in my view.

To hold otherwise would, in effect, limit the client to the retention of his original solicitor and would effectively prevent the client from discharging that solicitor prior to the completion of the matter. … The very nature of the arrangement between the parties precludes the existence of a lien for fees which are potential only and depend upon the successful outcome of the proceedings. . . . . .

Where a solicitor has no lien because of the nature of the fee arrangement or is precluded from asserting it because of the overriding consideration of the rights of the client, it is my view that the solicitor may, on being asked to transfer a file by a client, ask for and is entitled to receive an appropriate undertaking from the new solicitor in respect of his potential claim for fees and for any claim for disbursements.
In the later case, Marceau J. held that a solicitor's lien could be asserted in the context of a contingency arrangement.
He expressed concern about O'Leary J.'s finding that the prior solicitor was entitled to an undertaking from the subsequent solicitor and made the following comments at paras.

7, 10, 12 and 18–20: I have difficulty reconciling the proposition that no lien exists for a future contingency fee with the imposition of a trust obligation on the solicitor taking over the file which was the result in those circumstances. . . . . .
O'Leary J. did not specify any further ground for imposing trust conditions upon the new lawyer's conduct of the file which would ensure payment of the original firm's account. . . . . .
Stevenson, W.A. and Côté, J.E. in their Civil Procedure Guide (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1996) cite Doyle v.
Keats (1990), 46 B.C.L.R.
Master) for the proposition that a charging order may be made in these circumstances against the cause of action.
The authors have placed a “Quare”, in bold type, after this case.
In that case Master Wilson in British Columbia reasoned that by acting on the file the contingency lawyers had preserved a chose in action, the cause of action.

This basis for the order is perhaps more arguable where the limitation period has now passed and the lawyer truly preserved the cause of action by commencing it, but in this case another solicitor commenced the action so that argument is not available.
While it is true that preservation of the action requires the performance from time to time of steps in the action, and the action is property i.e. a chose in action, Doyle v.

Keats seems to be the first case allowing a charging order against property not yet identified. … The Master was of the view that extending the charge to a contingent judgment or settlement was a logical extension of the reasoning in the English cases… . . . . .
I agree with Master Wilson's approach that it is logical to extend the reasoning in the old English cases to include the fees of lawyers who today work under legally approved contingency agreements.

The order sought by the law firm, which would prevent payment by the defendant to the plaintiff of the fruits of litigation, be they ascertained in the future by way of settlement or judgment, without first allowing time for ascertainment of the account of the law firm and payment of same, is consistent with the principle that the court will protect solicitors for their fees provided this can be done without unduly interfering with the client's pursuit of his claim.

I cannot see that the client's lawsuit is in any way interfered with by ensuring that he does not take the proceeds of the lawsuit should it be successful without paying for the work done by his former solicitors. … I have now signed the order charging the proceeds of the lawsuit in favour of the law firm's account to be taxed when there is a settlement or judgment.
There has been surprisingly little judicial consideration of either of these cases.
O'Leary J.'s judgment was referred to by Pritchard J. of the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench in Merchant Law Group, Re, 209 Sask.
R.
However, solicitor's liens were not at issue in that case.

Rather, Pritchard J. relied upon O'Leary J.'s decision in concluding that Merchant Law Group could not require a client under a contingency arrangement to pay its outstanding account prior to transferring its file to another solicitor.
Marceau J.'s reasoning was endorsed in the very recent decision in Troelstra v.
Vos, 264 Sask.
R.
123, 2005 SKQB 98 (Sask.
There, the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench granted Merchant Law Group an order charging the chose in action of a former client in a matrimonial proceeding.

Marceau J.'s decision was also referred to by one of the parties in Cochard, Re, though that case did not involve a contingency arrangement.… Therefore, I conclude that Marceau J.'s approach is to be preferred and that funds arising from settlement or judgment in contingency matters are in principle property that can be attached by a charging order or charging lien.
Whether a charge will attach in a particular case will depend upon a consideration of all of the relevant factors.
Extent of Charge The third Laughlin criterion limits a charging order to fees and disbursements incurred in the same litigation that recovered or preserved the property.
A similar restriction appears to apply to charging liens.
Atkinson states at p.
43 that “this particular or special lien … extends to [the solicitor's] costs in the particular action or proceeding only”.
Further, he notes at p.
59 that “[t]he lien on funds does not extend to any debts but professional charges and disbursements due to the solicitor.

For example, he cannot assert any lien for money paid by him for his client even to pay off a lien due to the former solicitor, nor for money lent to the client.” In cases such as Cochard, Re where a law firm has conducted more than one matter on behalf of a client, the courts have been careful to restrict the charge to those fees and disbursements arising from the particular matter in which property was recovered or preserved….

Continued Existence of Fund Finally, an issue arises with respect to the property to be charged given that, in several of these cases, the personal injury lawsuits have been resolved and funds have been paid over to the clients by the Respondents.
The Respondents argue, in essence, that there is therefore no “fund” remaining to be attached by either a charging order or a charging lien.

The Applicant, for its part, argues that because the Respondents took their own fees out of the settlement or judgment proceeds before paying the remainder out to the clients, a portion of the “fund” remains and can be attached.
Resolution of whether this is so requires a consideration of how the charging order and charging lien attach to property and, in this context, the distinction between the two is critical.
The charging order, as discussed above, is a creature of statute.
Therefore, it can arise only pursuant to the statutory mechanism set out in Rule 625.
It is well established that, absent an application to the Court under that Rule, no charging order exists.

In Tots & Teens at 107, Henry J. quoted Lord Hanworth's statements in Mason that“[i]t is the solicitor's right to go to the court and to ask the court to charge property in his favour; until that is done, he has no right in it.” and that “[t]hat lien is one which prevails over a fund which is in sight; the right is one which, so to speak, cannot prevail at large.” In White Resource Management Ltd. v.
Durish (1997), 211 A.R.
376, (Alta.
Q.B.), Mason J. of this Court held at para.
17 that “[c]ounsel must specifically apply for a solicitor's lien under rule 625.” In Cochard, Re, Veit J. reviewed these cases and concluded at para.
79 that “[i]t is clear from the weight of case law and from authorities such as Atkinson, that, until the court grants a Rule 625 charge, the law firm has nothing.” She went on to hold at para.

111 that “[t]he potential exercise of that discretion to refuse a [Rule 625] charge, or set priorities, or reduce the amount of the charge from the amount claimed are precisely the reasons why, until a solicitor has a charge, she has nothing.” The Respondents argue that the absence of retrospective effect of Rule 625 means that once the fund generated by the lawsuit was paid over to the client, it ceased to exist in their hands and there is nothing at this point to which a charging order can attach.

This, however, begs the question given the Applicant's position that that portion of the fund which was paid to the Respondents for their fees continues to exist in their hands, allowing Rule 625 to have current effect.
Having said that, I am inclined to accept the Respondents' position.

To hold that a subsequent law firm is not free to deal with the proceeds of a client's settlement or judgment by taking its own fees and paying the remainder over to the client is, in my view, contrary to the accepted position that a law firm has nothing until a charging order actually has been granted.
The situation is less clear in respect of the charging lien.
Atkinson states at p.

9 that a charging lien, unlike a charging order, exists without a court order: [U]ntil the charging order is actually pronounced there is no charge in existence; in the words of Lord Selborne in Pinkerton v.

Easton[citation omitted], “The Legislature has not given a charge, but a power to the Court to create a charge, for a solicitor's costs, upon property recovered or preserved, when meritorious services of the solicitor have resulted in such recovery or preservation.” A lien on funds, on the contrary, is acquired by the solicitor ipso facto the moment property has been recovered or preserved by his proceedings.
Thus, a charging lien, unlike a charging order, appears to have some kind of retrospective effect.
The Applicant may not be precluded from claiming a charging lien solely on the grounds that the funds in question have been dispersed through payment to the Respondents and to the individual clients.
However, as I will discuss later in these reasons, the charging lien does not exist entirely independent of a court order.
Defences Even where there is found to be property that might properly be charged, there are defences available to resist the granting of a charge.
As the defences available in respect of a charging order are different from those available in respect of a charging lien, it will be convenient at this point to consider the two charges separately.
Charging Order—Limitation Period The Respondents argued that the Applicant is disentitled to a charging order by Rule 625(3) because its claim is barred by a limitation period.
It is clear from the terms of the Rule itself and from the case law that a claim for a charging order can be barred by a limitation period.
There appears to be no dispute that the applicable limitation period is two years.

However, the Respondents take the position that the limitation period begins to run when the client leaves the first law firm while the Applicant's position is that the limitation period does not begin until the client's matter has settled and a fund has arisen to which a charge could attach.
In light of Marceau J.'s decision that a solicitor's lien can arise in a contingency situation prior to the resolution of the underlying matter, I am inclined toward the Respondents' view.
However, in light of my conclusion on the next ground, I need not decide this issue.

Charging Order—Discretionary Nature Even if the claim for a charging order is not barred by a limitation period, the timing of the application is important given the discretionary nature of the charging order.
Rule 625 provides that the Court “may” grant a charging order and the case law is uniform in saying that doing so is in the discretion of the Court.
The fourth criterion enumerated by our Court of Appeal in Laughlin provides that the Court may refuse to grant a charging order if to do so would be unfair in the circumstances.
In this case, I find that granting the charging order would be unfair in light of the significant delay by Merchant Law Group in bringing this application.
The affidavit filed by Mr.
Perras attaches correspondence indicating that the clients in question left Merchant Law Group between 2001 and 2003.
Mr.
Perras deposes that the accounts sent to Vogel & Company by Merchant Law Group were dated between early 2002 and early 2004.
Yet the Originating Notice was not filed until May 31, 2004.

While this delay may or may not have put the Applicant outside the applicable limitation period, it would be unfair to expect the Respondents to have held back funds for such a length of time on the chance that an application for a charging order would be made.

I note that the Respondents were not in a position to force the Applicant's hand through a court application of their own; there is no application available to the Respondents which would require the Applicant to either apply for a charging order or decline to do so.

If the Applicant's arguments were accepted, the Respondents would be required to wait until the limitation period had expired before paying out settlement or judgment funds to themselves and their clients.
Surely the Court should not expect this to be the practice in personal injury lawsuits where clients expect to receive funds after settlement or judgment is reached.
Charging Lien—Requirement for Court Order Next I must consider the defences available in respect of the charging lien.
The Applicant seems to suggest that it is entitled to a charging lien solely by virtue of having done work on a matter.
To some extent, Atkinson supports this proposition.
As noted above, Atkinson states at p.
9 that a charging lien is acquired by the solicitor ipso facto when property has been recovered or preserved.
The case law, however, indicates that for a charging lien to be effective, it requires court sanction.

Indeed, as noted above, the lien is defined as the right to ask for the equitable intervention of the court to protect the solicitor's fees; clearly, the application to the court is a necessary part of obtaining this protection. … Similarly, Veit J. commented as follows in Cochard, Re, ¶ 70: Although Atkinson indicates that a solicitor's common law lien on funds is acquired by the lawyer ipso facto, it is clear from authorities including Atkinson and Halsbury's that a common law solicitor's lien must be recognized or formalized or approved by the court.
Charging Lien—Court's Discretion There is some suggestion in Atkinson that the granting of the court order formalizing the charging lien is not discretionary.
He states at p.

42 that “the lien on funds is still of considerable practical importance, notwithstanding the power to get a charging order, first, because, the power of the Court to give a charging order is discretionary, and not a matter of right…”.
However, given that the nature of the charging lien is a right to seek the equitable intervention of the Court, this cannot be so.
This was recognized by Veit J. at para.

70 of Cochard, Re as follows: Despite the broad wording used in the first Atkinson extract to refer to the common law lien, there is no doubt that the court maintains a discretion, which must of course be exercised judicially, in determining whether the common law lien would be recognized.
Thus, while the charging lien may arise ipso facto from a solicitor's efforts, the solicitor does not have an unassailable right to have that lien given effect by the Court.
Charging Lien—Limitations and Laches It is clear from the authorities, including Atkinson, that the charging lien is not subject to any statute of limitations.
Nevertheless, the equitable nature of the Court's intervention means that equitable defences may be raised.
For example, if there has been excessive delay in bringing the application, the defence of laches may apply.
Veit J. specifically noted this at para.

70 of Cochard, Re, saying that: [W]hile the common law lien is not subject to the statute of limitations, yet it is clear that a court may refuse to exercise its equitable interference on behalf of a lawyer if the lawyer has delayed excessively in bringing forward a claim for the lien.

Atkinson himself seems to recognize this, saying the following at p 60: But although the statutes are not a bar, it does not follow that the solicitor can be as dilatory as he pleases with impunity, for where his delay has been excessive, and the rights of other persons have suffered in consequence, the Court may refuse to exercise its equitable interference on his behalf or at least refuse to give him the costs of the application.

Charging Lien—Notice to Subsequent Solicitor … It seems to me that the Applicant's argument attempts to elevate mere notice of its claim to a duty on the part of the Respondents to ensure that the Applicant receives payment.

In my view, while solicitors are duty-bound to extend reasonable courtesies to one another, there is no such duty to ensure payment of another solicitor's account absent some intervention by the Court. … Moreover, characterizing the charging lien as the imposition of a duty on one solicitor by another is inconsistent with the requirement discussed above that the charging lien be, in Veit J.'s words, “recognized or formalized or approved” by the Court.
I read the following comments from Atkinson at pp.

42 and 82 to mean that notice to a subsequent solicitor that a prior solicitor intends to invoke a charging lien is a necessary but not a sufficient prerequisite to obtaining the lien's protection: The Court will exercise this equitable interference where the solicitor has given the opposite party or his solicitor notice of his lien, and that he claims the amount payable to his client to be paid to him in the first instance, in which case the opposite party will at his peril pay the client or release the claim, or compromise it without the assent of the solicitor. . . . . .

Although a notice of the solicitor's lien is not strictly a remedy, but merely a precautionary step before exercising a remedy, it may be convenient here to remind the practitioner of the importance of giving notice of the lien to any person who is about to compromise or pay any money to the client direct.
In fact, the moment the solicitor suspects the bona fides of his client he ought to give notice of his lien to the opposite party and his solicitor.
I do not, however, wish to imply that notice is a meaningless formality.
If a successor solicitor were to act in bad faith and, for example, disperse the settlement or judgment funds immediately upon receiving the notice, the equities might well be different.
That, however, is not the case here.

Charging Lien—Suggested Procedure The Applicant expressed the concern that, unless notice to a subsequent solicitor is enough to give rise to a charge on settlement or judgment proceeds, a practice could develop whereby a subsequent solicitor, having done even minimal work on a contingency file, could collect a contingency fee without any obligation toward the prior solicitor.
While I have no reason to think that such a practice is or is likely to become widespread, the concern is not without foundation.
Therefore, I think it prudent to set out the procedure by which charging liens should be invoked.
I pause to say that this procedure is limited to charging liens, it being clear that charging orders may be obtained only by application to the Court under Rule 625.
I also caution practitioners that this procedure will apply only in contingency arrangements.
Where there is no contingency agreement, a solicitor is not required, by virtue of Marceau J.'s analysis in A Client v.
A Law Firm, to wait until the conclusion of a lawsuit to tax his account and obtain his fees from a departed client.
As discussed above, as a necessary precondition to obtaining the protection of a charging lien, a prior solicitor must give his successor notice of his intention to invoke the lien.
While I have stated that I do not believe the use of particular words to be necessary, this notice should make clear to the successor solicitor that a charging lien is claimed.
The lien must then be perfected by order of the Court.
Pursuant to Marceau J.'s analysis, the prior solicitor may proceed with that application without waiting for the lawsuit to be resolved.

If the prior solicitor does not proceed immediately with that application, the successor solicitor is under an obligation not to dispose of the settlement or judgment funds without advising his predecessor.

Once the successor solicitor is ready to disperse the funds, he must notify the prior solicitor of his intention to do so and give the prior solicitor some reasonable period of time, depending upon the circumstances, in which to bring an application for perfection of the charging lien.
If the prior solicitor does so in a timely fashion, the Court will of course deal with the application.
If he does not, the lien is unperfected and therefore without effect and the successor solicitor may disperse the funds without further regard to the claim.
I recognize that this procedure puts the onus on the prior solicitor to bring the matter before the Court.
That is as it should be.
As I mentioned in the context of the charging order, there is no application available to a successor solicitor to force the prior solicitor to take the necessary application to perfect his lien.

Particularly in light of the fact that charging liens are not subject to statutes of limitation, the successor solicitor cannot be required to wait indefinitely for the prior solicitor to take action.
Rawlins J.'s analysis was referred to with approval by McMahon J. in Calf Robe v.
Canada (Attorney General), 2006 ABQB 652, 2006 CarswellAlta 1158, 405 A.R.
366 at paragraph 19.
Determining Priority of Solicitors' Liens If a lawyer seeks a declaration of priority in respect of his or her charging order lien, the lawyer must have first applied for such a lien under R.
625: … an application for priority of solicitors' liens is premature when counsel have not yet applied for liens.
White Resource Management Ltd. v.
Durish (1997), 54 Alta.
L.R.
214, per Mason J.
Chargeable Interest The charge relates to the whole property, not just to the client's interest in it.
Rule 625 does not say the charge can relate only to the interest of the client in the property.
The charge is “upon the property recovered or preserved” through the instrumentality of the solicitor.

I agree with the decisions cited, which state that the charge can extend to the interest of any person in the property, whether or not he is the client and whether or not he was a party to the action.
In Bloomaert Martin J.A., states at pp.

275–276: Prior to the passing of this Act, the right of a solicitor to a lien upon the funds recovered or preserved through his exertions was well recognized in courts of equity … This Imperial statutory provision is in force in Saskatchewan, and must be given full force in matters of practice and procedure in our courts.

Under its provisions, the court has power, in any proceedings, to make a charging order in favour of the solicitor employed against any property recovered or preserved through the solicitor's instrumentality, in respect of his taxed costs; and it has been frequently held that a charge may be granted not only upon the interest in the preserved property of those by whom the solicitor is employed, but upon the interests of others interested in the preserved property who get the benefit.
In Greer v.
Young (1883), 24 Ch.
D.

545 … it was held by the Court of Appeal that the fact that the parties beneficially entitled are not parties to the action, is quite immaterial if the fund has been recovered or preserved for their benefit.
In that case, Brett, M.R., at p.

918, expresses his view in these words: (I think) the fundamental theory of the section is the idea that what has been recovered by the action of the solicitor is to be treated as if it were salvage ** and to be paid for on the theory that a salvage service has been rendered.
In Leacock v.
McLaren (1894), 9 Man.
R.

599, it was held by the full Court of Manitoba that, if there was property recovered or preserved, the solicitor is entitled to an order giving him a charge for his costs, even though other persons have become interested in it … I agree with that … In short, the charge attaches to whosever interests in the property is preserved by the solicitor's successful action.
Akins v.
Carraher (1987), 76 A.R.
249 ((Master)), at 264–65, per Master Funduk.
Assuming no fraud and collusion between the parties, the solicitor's lien only attaches to what is left after proper set-off between the parties has been applied.
In White Resource Management Ltd. v.
Durish (1997), 54 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 207 (Q.B.), Mason J. said, at p.
216: … counsel has a right to a solicitor's lien subject to the prior rights of the parties to set-off.

Or stated alternatively, counsel is entitled to lien on the net benefits (the balance which remains owing after set-off) achieved for his or her client. . . . . . … it is clear that a solicitor's lien is nothing more than an equitable right that stands no higher than the client's rights.
The solicitor's lien is, therefore, limited by whatever rights may be exercised against the client, even though the client cannot imperil or affect the solicitor's rights.
The following propositions appear to apply:
(1) a solicitor's lien is nothing more than a [sic] equitable right against funds or property recovered by counsel for the client
(2) that equitable right may not be alienated by the client's unilateral action
(3) the right is limited and stands no higher than the client's rights at law; and

(4) if it is just and equitable between the parties, set-off should have priority, unless there is fraud or some collusion practised upon counsel to defeat his or her equitable right, or unless counsel can claim a superior right at equity to the claim being made against the client.
Solicitor's Lien when File Is Transferred to New Counsel Practical instruction regarding the mechanics of succession of contingent-fee-files is, from my experience, hard to find.
Fortunately, a decision of the Honourable Mr.
Justice O'Leary in Law Firm v.
Solicitor (June 19, 1992), Doc.
No.
1242 (Alta.
Q.B.)] addresses, amongst others, two issues which may be of assistance in the transfer of Ms.
Buko's file to a new solicitor.

The O'Leary decision—as most people respectfully refer to it—gives detailed and comprehensive directions regarding the circumstances under which a lawyer may and may not maintain a solicitor's lien on the transfer of a file which is subject to the terms of a contingent fee agreement.
In short, the decision states: 1.
Under no circumstances is a lawyer justified or entitled to maintain a solicitor's lien on fees in a contingency arrangement.
Why?

The fees are “potential only and depend upon the successful outcome of the proceedings.” And, to allow a lien would “limit the client to the retention of [the] original solicitor and would effectively prevent the client from discharging that solicitor.” 2.
A lawyer is justified in maintaining a lien on disbursements whether the client is impliedly or explicitly responsible to pay them periodically or at the end.

Silence as to whom is to pay for disbursements is an “inference that the client will ultimately be responsible for them.” When the contract specifically provides that the firm's expenses are to be paid out of any recovery it secures, the firm has no lien on the disbursements either.

3. “Superimposed on the legal principles relating to solicitor's liens are the ethical considerations… If insistence on the lien by the solicitor would deprive the client of the right to freely choose the solicitor to represent him, then as a matter of ethics the right of the client should prevail over the claim of the solicitor to a lien.”Buko v.
Belzerowski Law Office (1998), 62 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 260 (Q.B.), at 264–65, per Christensen T.O.
In Client v.
Law Firm (1999), 74 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 257 (Q.B.), a law firm and a client had entered into a contingency fee agreement.
Prior to the completion of the litigation, the law firm filed a notice of ceasing to act.
The law firm sought an order protecting it for its fees.
Marceau J. said, at pp.
261–62: Clearly the common law and later statutes in England … as well as … R.

625(1) of our Rules of Court all have one object: ensuring that a lawyer who has laboured on a litigation file should not be deprived of a proper fee because his former client seeks to be paid the fruits of that litigation without paying the lawyer.
I mention in passing that the Client may be unable to pay the solicitor for reasons beyond his control such as a third party garnishee or being petitioned into bankruptcy.
The order sought does not require any finding of bad faith on the part of the Client.
I agree … that it is logical to extend the reasoning in the old English cases to include the fees of lawyers who today work legally under legally approved contingency agreements.

The order sought by the Law Firm, which would prevent payment by the Defendant to the Plaintiff of the fruits of litigation, be they ascertained in the future by way of settlement or judgment, without first allowing time for ascertainment of the account of the Law Firm and payment of same, is consistent with the priniciple that the Court will protect solicitors for their fees provided this can be done without unduly interfering with the client's pursuit of his claim.

I cannot see that the client's lawsuit is in any way interefered with by ensuring that he does not take the proceeds of the lawsuit should it be successful without paying for the work done by his former solicitors.
To allay the client's concerns about the other litigant using the information contained in the documents filed in respect of this application, Marceau J. sealed those document until further order.
Rule 10.4(5) “Unfairness” In Paragon Capital Corporation Ltd v.
Starke Dominion Ltd, 2020 ABCA 216, 2020 CarswellAlta 979, 6 Alta.
L.R.

224, the majority of the Court of Appeal panel noted that the “unfairness” referred to in Rule 10.4(5) is unfairness which would arise from the granting of the order, not a refusal to grant the order.

The Court said: [52] Paragon argues that even if the chambers judge had discretion to grant the conditional order, he did so in error based on his misapplication of r 10.4(5) which reads: “An order must not be made under this rule if in all the circumstances the Court considers that to make the order would be unfair”.
The chambers judge, however, found in para 54 of his decision that “…New Rules r 10.4(5) adds a fairness element to this Court's analysis.
This court finds that it would be unfair to dismiss BDP's application on this factor alone”.
[53] In other words, the chambers judge improperly applied r 10.4(5) to consider whether unfairness would arise from refusing the order, rather than from granting it.
We agree that this was an error of law allowing us to review his decision on the standard of correctness …

paragraphs.text: (1) A lawyer may make an agreement with a client about the amount and manner of payment of the whole or any part of past or future lawyer's charges for services performed by the lawyer. (2) The amount a lawyer is to be paid may be determined in any appropriate way, including (a) a gross sum, (b) commission, (c) percentage, (d) salary, or (e) an hourly rate. (3) The amount payable may be at the same or at a greater or lesser rate than the rate to which the lawyer would be entitled under rule 10.2 if no retainer agreement were entered into.

paragraphs.text: (1) In a retainer agreement or otherwise, a provision is void if the provision (a) purports to relieve a lawyer from liability for negligence or any other liability to which the lawyer might be subject as a lawyer, or (b) purports to provide that an action, application or proceeding cannot be abandoned, discontinued or settled without a lawyer's consent. paragraphs.text: (1) A contingency fee agreement must (a) be in writing, and (b) be signed by the lawyer and the lawyer's client or by their authorized agents. (2) To be enforceable, a contingency fee agreement must contain the following particulars in precise and understandable terms: (a) the name and address of each client; (b) the name and address of the lawyer; (c) a statement of the nature of the claim; (d) a statement of the event or contingency on which the lawyer's fees are to be paid to the lawyer; (e) a statement about (i) the manner in which the contingency fee is to be calculated, provided that no fee, calculated as a percentage or otherwise, may be payable on disbursements or other charges recovered, (ii) the maximum fee payable, or the maximum rate calculated, detailing the disbursements and other charges that are included in that fee or rate or indicating that disbursements and other charges are in addition to that fee or rate, and (iii) whether the client is responsible to pay disbursements and other charges, and if so, a general description of the types of disbursements and other charges likely to be incurred, other than relatively minor disbursements; (f) if the lawyer is to receive any amount from a costs award, a statement that (i) the cost award is intended to be a complete or partial reimbursement of the lawyer's charges to the client, (ii) the cost award is owned by the client and that by signing the contingency fee agreement the client is waiving the right to any amount from the costs award that is payable to the lawyer in accordance with subclause (iv), (iii) the amount from the costs award retained by the lawyer will be in addition to the lawyer's percentage, fixed fees or other form of legal fees, and (iv) the percentage of the costs award that the lawyer may receive may not exceed the percentage of the judgment or settlement that the lawyer is entitled to; (g) a statement that, if the client gives notice in writing to the lawyer within 5 days after the client's copy of the contingency fee agreement is served on the client, the client may terminate the contingency fee agreement without incurring any liability for the lawyer's fees, but that the client is liable to reimburse the lawyer for reasonable disbursements; (h) a statement that (i) at the request of the client, a review officer may review either or both of the contingency fee agreement and any lawyer's charges in an account rendered under the agreement, and (ii) either or both of the contingency fee agreement or any lawyer's charges may be further reviewed by way of an appeal from a review officer's decision to a judge. (3) The contingency fee agreement must be witnessed by a person who sees the client sign the agreement, and that person must then swear an affidavit of execution. (4) The client must be served with a copy of the signed contingency fee agreement within 10 days after the date on which the agreement is signed, and an affidavit of service to that effect must be executed by the person who served the agreement. (5) A client may terminate a contingency fee agreement without incurring any liability for the lawyer's fees under the agreement if the client, within 5 days after service on the client of the copy of the contingency fee agreement, gives written notice of the termination to the lawyer, but the client is liable to reimburse the lawyer for reasonable disbursements incurred by the lawyer. (6) If a contingency fee agreement provides that a lawyer is entitled to an amount from a costs award, the lawyer is not entitled to receive from the costs award any higher percentage of the judgment or settlement than the lawyer is entitled to receive under the contingency fee agreement. (7) Every account rendered under a contingency fee agreement must contain a statement that at the client's request a review officer may determine both the reasonableness of the account and the reasonableness of the contingency fee agreement. (8) An account that does not contain the statement required by subrule (7) is of no effect unless the Court (a) is satisfied (i) that the omission of the statement was inadvertent, and (ii) the client has not been misled or prejudiced, and (b) the Court waives the requirement for the statement. Alta. Reg. 128/2015, s. 8

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.7:1 Rule 10.7 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.7. 1. Overview In Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation v. Rath and Company Barristers and Solicitors, 2024 ABKB 258, Justice Simard set out the Court’s approach to Rule 10.7: [16] The aim of contingency fees is to make court proceedings available to people who could not otherwise afford to have their legal rights determined. This goal should be encouraged and a flexible approach should be taken to problems arising from contingency fee arrangements, in order to facilitate access to the courts for more Canadians: MS v DM, 2014 ABQB 702 at para 37. It is also the case, however, that the people who rely on contingency fee agreements “are often vulnerable due to poverty, impact of injuries, educational status or other social disadvantages” and the Rules of Court and other rules governing contingency fee agreements offer some protection to this potentially vulnerable group: MS at para 38. Therefore, when a court is interpreting a contingency fee agreement or considering its fairness, “the necessity and importance of encouraging this form of legal fee arrangement should be balanced with the need to safeguard the citizens who rely on contingency fee agreements in order to have access to justice.”: MS at para 39. The Court’s Approach to Rule 10.7 Cases [17] While a flexible and balanced approach is called for when interpreting contingency fee agreements and deciding whether they are fair or reasonable, it does not apply with the same force, or to the same effect, in cases considering the mandatory requirements in the Rules of Court: MS at para 52. The language in Rule 10.7 and 10.8 is very clear and is mandatory: certain things “must” be in contingency fee agreements and contingency fee accounts, and certain procedures “must” be followed. If those things are not present or those procedures are not followed, the Rules state clearly that the contingency fee agreement is not enforceable. [18] Among the reasons for following a less flexible approach in these cases is that “Rule 10.7 is a consumer protection provision; it sets out requirements to ensure that the terms of the contingency fee are clear and to ensure that the client has executed and been provided with a copy of the agreement”: Barry v Industrial Alliance and Financial Services, 2022 ABKB 706 at para 13. Also, the requirements of Rule 10.7 “are not onerous and are easily incorporated into contingency agreements”: Stanchfield v Doe, 2023 ABKB 273 at para 21. [19] While the Court’s approach in Rule 10.7 cases is “less” flexible, that does not mean there is no flexibility whatsoever. This Court has drawn a line between “minor” or “technical” non-compliance with the Rules, from which it can grant relief, and more “serious” or “substantive” non-compliance with the Rules, which will be fatal to an agreement. The Court has articulated this distinction in slightly different ways: (a) “I agree that Rule 618 [the predecessor Rule to Rule 10.7] purposefully prohibits enforcement when there is non-compliance, but I find that the Rule should not be interpreted so inflexibly that the most minuscule and immaterial omission would prevent the enforcement of the agreement. Therefore, even though I confirm that defects in a contingency agreement will be strictly construed against the lawyer, the court is not without its judicial discretion to alleviate against minor technical oversights that are without import”: per Germain J in Sonnenberg v Schumacher & Associates, 2005 ABQB 352 at para 38; (b) “the flexible approach is more appropriate when considering more minor or technical departures from the rules”: MS at para 52; and (c) “In cases where the non-compliance is not minor or technical but undermines the client protection and clarity the rules are designed to create, courts must be careful not to reward counsel, or prejudice clients, for counsel’s non-compliance.”: Stanchfield at para 21. [20] As noted recently by Graesser J in Mikisew Cree First Nation v Rath, 2023 ABKB 321 at para 86, “there is no bright line between minor and substantial irregularities”. Each case will turn on its specific facts. 2. The formal procedure mandated by Rules 10.7(2)(g), (3), and (4) In Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation v. Rath and Company Barristers and Solicitors, 2024 ABKB 258, Justice Simard set out the procedure required by Rules 10.7(2)(g) and Rules 10.7(3) and (4): [69] When they are read together, subrules 10.7(2)(g), (3) and (4) mandate a cohesive formal procedure for what is to happen when a contingency fee agreement is executed, and immediately afterwards: (a) a person other than the client must be present when the client signs the agreement, and that person must then complete an affidavit of execution. This adds heightened solemnity and formality to the signing of such agreements, providing an outward reminder to both parties of the extraordinary nature of contingency fee agreements, and the important consequences of signing them. The swearing of the affidavit of execution also ensures that there can be no dispute about the date on which the agreement was signed, which triggers service, the next step in the process; (b) the lawyer must then serve the agreement on the client within 10 days after the agreement is executed. In my view, the Court must place importance on the Legislature’s choice of the word “served” in Rule 10.7(4). The Rule does not say that the lawyer is to “deliver”, “give” or “send to” the client a fully-executed copy of the agreement. The lawyer must serve the agreement on the client, then complete an affidavit of service. Those words clearly connote formal service. I will address the issue of what particular type of service is required, below; (c) the lawyer formally serving their client with a fully-executed copy of a contingency agreement will again impress on the client the heightened solemnity and importance of what it has agreed to and, even more importantly, it may draw to the client’s attention its right to terminate the agreement without penalty, within five days after being “served”, i.e. the exact statement in the agreement that is mandated by Rule 10.7(2)(g) (I note that the client’s substantive right to terminate is provided in Rule 10.7(5). Rule 10.7(2)(g) does not create the termination right; rather it requires the lawyer to insert notice of that termination right in the agreement). Obviously, if the mandated statement is not present in the agreement, formal service by the lawyer is less likely to fulfil this purpose; (d) the lawyer must then complete an affidavit of service, which performs the important function of ensuring that there can be no dispute about when the client was served, starting the five-day optional termination period, and when the termination right expired; and (e) the client has five days after being served with the executed agreement, to give written notice of termination to the lawyer. If the client terminates in this period, the client will not incur any liability for the contingency fee but will be liable only for reasonable disbursements. If the client does not terminate in this five-day period, it will be obligated to pay the contingency fee. … [73] Subrules 10.7(2)(g) and 10.7(4) use the terms “served” and “service” but they do not specify what type of service is required. Our Court of Appeal addressed the concept of service in Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corporation, 2012 ABCA 266, a dispute about whether claim disallowances in a bankruptcy had been properly served. The Court commented at paras 18 – 19: The legal concept of service was discussed in Zahmol Properties Ltd. v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at paras. 14-6, 522 AR 32: Service is a specialized form of notice. While “notice” is sometimes used as a synonym for “knowledge”, in this context notice encompasses the conveying of knowledge or information with intention to affect legal rights. For example, the exercise of an option in a contract conveys the information that the contractual right is being exercised, and that the legal rights of the optionor and the optionee will be affected. A casual statement of an intention to exercise the option at a future time may convey “knowledge”, but not in a way that fixes legal rights. The concept is illustrated by the decision in St. Peter’s Evangelical Lutheran Church v. Ottawa, 1982 CanLII 60 (SCC), [1982] 2 SCR 616. By statute a municipality could prevent the demolition of a historic building, provided that notice that the municipality did not consent to the demolition was given within 90 days. The council of the municipality adopted a resolution within the 90 days, denying permission to demolish the building. The owners of the building were aware of the resolution, because two of its representatives were present when the resolution was passed, and it was reported in the newspapers, but no formal notice of the resolution was ever given. While conceding that no formal notice had been given, the municipality argued that the actual knowledge of the resolution was “notice in fact”. The Supreme Court of a ruled at p. 629 that it was an error to equate “knowledge on the part of the appellants with notice given by the respondent City”. The Court held that some type of “notice” to fix the legal rights of the parties was needed in addition to mere knowledge of the resolution. Service of legal process conveys the information that an action or proceeding has been commenced that may affect the rights of the person being served, with an intention to affect or engage legal rights. The party served is put on notice that it must take steps to protect its rights, or the court or tribunal might adjudicate in its absence. Sometimes legal processes are commenced in order to crystallize rights, without a final decision having been made as to whether the action will be triggered by service and prosecuted. Sometimes knowledge of an action or proceeding is conveyed without intending to affect legal rights, as when a “courtesy copy” of legal process is provided. Where the knowledge of the legal process is conveyed without an intention to affect legal rights, there is generally no “service”: Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223 at paras. 103-7, 34 Alta LR (4th) 199; Bennett v. Cultural Tours (1991), 58 BCLR (2d) 225. In order to demonstrate proper service of the disallowances of the claims, it must be shown that the respondents received notice of the disallowances of their claims, in a context that made it clear that their rights were being engaged. [74] Thus, it is apparent that service is a somewhat flexible concept. However, the core requirement is that the party being served receives effective notice that their legal rights may be affected. As I noted above, one of the important purposes of the service required by Rule 10.4 is that the client is effectively notified or reminded of their right to terminate a contingency fee agreement within the cooling off period. Because the notice mandated in Rule 10.7(2)(g) must state that the termination period commences when the client is “served”, it follows logically that when a client receives a fully-executed contingency agreement from their lawyer under Rule 10.4, the client must be made to understand that it has been “served”. Only if it knows that it has been served will it know that its five-day termination period has started running. Therefore, at a minimum, to comply with Rule 10.4, a lawyer’s correspondence to their client must expressly use the term “served” or “service”.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.8 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: If a lawyer does not comply with rule 10.7(1) to (4), (6) and (7), the lawyer is, on successful accomplishment or disposition of the subject-matter of the contingency fee agreement, entitled only to lawyer's charges determined in accordance with rule 10.2 as if no contingency fee agreement had been entered into.
